transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-09-02 15:30 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen, Jonah Price, Priya Singh (Redwood); Rafael Ortega, Dana Li, Samir Patel, Olga Petrova (Nimbus)

Summary (auto): Handoff from AE to CSM/SE, clarify network and security requirements for private deployment, define pilot scope and timelines.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this deal. We wanted to do a quick handoff to Priya and Jonah and run through the implementation plan. Rafael, Dana, are you both on?
[00:08] Rafael: Yeah, I'm here, thanks.
[00:10] Dana: Here, thanks Maya.
[00:12] Samir: Samir is here.
[00:14] Olga: Olga as well.
[00:18] Maya: Great. Quick agenda — we'll do intros, handoff context, SE covers the private deploy options and network bits, security Q&A, then next steps. Jonah, over to you for the technical overview?
[00:28] Jonah: Cool. Uh, hi everyone — Jonah Price, Solutions Eng. I'll try to keep it high level first then we can drop into specifics. So, Nimbus, you told us you're planning for an initial pilot for search re-ranking and chat-like support in a closed dataset, correct?
[00:40] Dana: Correct, initial focus is support assistants and a reranker for internal docs. We'll want relatively low latency — sub 200ms p50 if possible — but throughput is not huge to start, maybe 10 to 30 qps.
[00:54] Jonah: Got it. That maps well to Redwood Dedicated or Private depending on whether you want the control plane be private. From our side there are two main deployment shapes: Hosted API (fastest), Dedicated (reserved Redwood-managed capacity), and Private (VPC or on-prem with customer-managed network). For strict data residency and audit controls you were leaning Private, Olga?
[01:16] Olga: Yes, for now legal wants the control plane isolated. We need to make sure logs and keys never leave our environment, and KMS/HSM integration is mandatory. Also SOC 2 artifacts and some vendor security questionnaires.
[01:28] Maya: Right, that's why Priya on CS will be your main point for onboarding. Priya, would you like to describe the typical onboarding milestones?
[01:34] Priya: Sure. Hi everyone, Priya Singh. We usually do a discovery -> network validation -> pilot -> scale pattern. Discovery: gather traffic profiles, sequences, token length distribution. Network: validate VPC peering, firewall rules, and route tables. Pilot: small scale smoke tests, end-to-end checks, and perf bench. Then scale. We'll propose checkpoints and runbooks.
[01:52] Rafael: On traffic profiles — Samir will prepare sample payloads but fyi our average prompt length is about 120 tokens, and expected peak is closer to 25 qps with spikes to 50 qps for short windows.
[02:05] Samir: Yep, I'll get that to you.
[02:07] Jonah: Perfect — that helps sizing. For the Private option, there are two network models: 1) Customer-managed VPC with peering to Redwood control plane endpoints; 2) Full on-prem air-gapped using our private bundle. The first is most common and supports KMS integrations via customer KMS endpoints and HSM proxies. We have a checklist for required open ports and IP ranges.
[02:29] Dana: Do you support direct peering or only transit?
[02:32] Jonah: We support both; depending on your cloud provider we can do VPC peering, PrivateLink for AWS, or Azure Private Endpoint. There's also a hybrid where compute lives in your VPC and the control plane is a private tenant in our region.
[02:45] Olga: For compliance, we can't have logs forwarded to a third-party unless they're encrypted and we hold keys. Does Redwood allow customer-controlled encryption keys?
[02:54] Jonah: Yes, we support customer-managed keys (KMS) and HSM integrations for the Private deployment path. There is an agent that runs in your VPC to handle key-wrap and audit logging. Note: the agent needs outbound HTTPS to the Redwood control endpoint for heartbeats, but payload data can be pinned to internal peering.
[03:13] Rafael: You said "agent" — is that a daemon we install? Any compatibility issues with our RedHat nodes?
[03:18] Jonah: It's a light-weight containerized agent; we've tested on common Linux distros including RHEL, Ubuntu, and EKS. Occasionally, customers hit kernel-level TLS differences, but our docs cover libc/openssl caveats.
[03:29] [03:30] Speaker 1: Mm-hmm.
[03:32] Maya: Quick question on timelines — when could a pilot realistically start if we get contractual sign-off this week?
[03:36] Priya: With a standard cadence we'd aim to start network validation within 3 business days of receiving VPC details. If there are no major network blockers, pilot readiness within two weeks is achievable. So roughly 10 business days end-to-end to pilot, more if audit docs take longer.
[03:52] Dana: That sounds ok. For the pilot success criteria — we want p50 latency under 250ms and memory/throughput stability during a two-hour soak at 30 qps. Also we need proof that PII is not retained and that logs can be purged on demand.
[04:08] Jonah: Understood. We'll run an internal bench with a configuration that matches your token distribution and provide a reproducible script. We'll also show KV cache warmup behavior and how batching is tuned.
[04:20] Samir: On the topic of batching — we observed on other vendors that batching caused latency spikes. How do you guarantee tail latency won't explode?
[04:27] Jonah: Great question. Our runtime uses continuous batching and dynamic priority scheduling. For low-latency slices we can pin a small pool for single-request fast-paths and a separate batch pool for throughput. You can tune the per-route SLOs. There may be trade-offs to throughput but we can size appropriately for the pilot.
[04:45] Olga: Security questionnaires — we already filled some of your vendor sheets in the RFP. We'll need SOC2 AICPA report and your key rotation policy. Where do we get those?
[04:55] Maya: I'll send the security packet. Jonah, can you drop the SOC2 link and key rotation whitepaper into the shared drive?
[04:59] Jonah: Yep, I'll upload a link to the file. Also, note that for Private deployments we provide a per-tenant audit log that you can keep on-prem. There is a config flag for log retention and immediate purge endpoints for compliance.
[05:14] Dana: Good. On RBAC and SSO — do you integrate with our Okta SAML for admin access?
[05:19] Priya: Yes, we support SAML/Okta for the Redwood Console access and fine-grained RBAC. For Private, the console can be run as a customer-hosted control plane and connected to your IdP.
[05:30] Rafael: A tactical question: for model versions, can we pin a model to a specific quantized variant? We want determinism across runs for evaluation.
[05:36] Jonah: You can pin to a model artifact version and a runtime profile (e.g., float16 baseline vs int8 quantized). We'll give you the performance profiles and token-cost estimates for each. For deterministic outputs, you can also pin seeds and disable sampling.
[05:49] [06:00] Maya: There's a question in the chat about benchmarks — do you have any public numbers for the models we'll likely use?
[06:06] Jonah: We have an internal benchmark sheet — I'll share anonymized perf numbers for a 2k-context reranker and a 1k chat model. I'll also add the latency/cost tradeoff table.
[06:16] Dana: Great. Any gotchas you seen in prior customers during network validation?
[06:21] Jonah: Most are firewall rules and DNS resolution — the agent needs to reach specific hostnames and sometimes corporate proxies block them. Also some orgs have strict egress rules that break the heartbeats; we handle via proxy configuration but it adds time. Another thing: if you use custom KMS that requires VPC endpoints, make sure the endpoints are routable from the agent.
[06:41] Samir: We'll get our network team to double-check.
[06:44] Olga: On data lineage — can you show us how audit logs map to request ids and which artifact stores the artifacts?
[06:50] Jonah: Yes, every request is tagged with a tracking id and trace headers. For Private, logs are written locally to your S3 bucket or internal object store — we support S3-compatible endpoints.
[07:02] [07:15] Dana: Ok so next steps recap?
[07:18] Maya: I'll summarize: Jonah to share runbook and perf sheet by Friday (2025-09-05). Priya to send onboarding timeline and scheduled check-ins. Samir to provide payload and traffic samples by 2025-09-08. Olga to forward compliance questions and required artifact list by 2025-09-10. We'll schedule a pre-pilot network validation week of 2025-09-15.
[07:37] Rafael: Sounds good. One more thing — pricing model for Dedicated vs Private — any ballpark numbers for committed capacity?
[07:44] Maya: For early pilots we usually do a short-term reserved pool or a burstable setup. I'll send a pricing sheet; big determinants are GPU class and concurrency. Jonah, can you attach typical TCO guidance?
[07:55] Jonah: Yep, will include. Note that quantization can lower TCO significantly, we'll provide cost-per-1k-tokens estimates under each profile.
[08:05] [08:30] Speaker 2: Uh-huh.
[08:32] Priya: I'll set up the follow-up calendar invites for the pre-pilot validation and kickoff. Any preferred times?
[08:38] Samir: Mornings are better for our APAC team, but we can be flexible.
[08:43] Dana: Let's aim for 09:30 PT during the week of the 15th.
[08:48] Maya: Perfect. If there are no other blockers, we'll close. Thanks everyone.
[08:52] Rafael: Thanks, talk soon.
[08:54] Olga: Thanks all.
